```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
```

# Model and source

```{r model-meta, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
ui <- rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Guk_2017_bodyWeight"))
cat("* Citation: ", ui$reference, "\n", sep = "")
cat("* Article (open access, PMC7042011): <https://doi.org/10.12793/tcp.2017.25.2.101>\n")
```

Guk 2017 is not a drug model. It is a **body-weight covariate model** for
children: a curve of weight against postmenstrual age (PMA, gestational age
plus postnatal age) fitted to one weight per child from 83,014 Korean pediatric
patients. The authors intended it for imputing missing weights when PMA is
known, and for simulating weight as a time-varying covariate in pediatric
pharmacokinetic studies.

The final model (Eq. 2) multiplies a sigmoid (Hill) function of PMA by a
logistic function of PMA:

$$
\mathrm{BW} = \frac{W_{\max}\,\mathrm{PMA}^{\gamma}}{\mathrm{PMA}_{50}^{\gamma} + \mathrm{PMA}^{\gamma}}
\times \frac{1}{e^{-\alpha\,\mathrm{PMA}} + \beta/\alpha}
$$

The sigmoid describes the rapid perinatal and infant growth; it has saturated
by about two years of age. The logistic factor describes the slower growth of
childhood and tends to $\alpha/\beta$ at large PMA. All parameters except the
logistic rate $\alpha$ differ between boys and girls (Table 2). Each child
contributed one weight, so no between-subject variability was estimated; the
residual error is proportional.

In the packaged model the rxode2 `time` variable **is** PMA in weeks, and the
output `bw` is body weight in kg. `SEXF` (1 = girl, 0 = boy) is required.

# Population

```{r population, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
pop <- ui$population
for (nm in names(pop)) cat("* **", nm, "**: ", paste(pop[[nm]], collapse = "; "), "\n", sep = "")
```

The data are electronic medical records from Severance Hospital, Seoul, from
January 2012 to March 2017: 83,014 patients younger than 12 years with one
weight each (Methods, Data; Table 1). Where gestational age was missing, the
child was assumed to have been born at term (40 weeks). The median PMA was
193.9 weeks (range 24.6 to 718.3) and the median weight 14.0 kg (range 0.4 to
97.0); 56.7% were boys.

# Source trace

Each `ini()` entry in `inst/modeldb/endogenous/Guk_2017_bodyWeight.R` has an
in-file comment giving its origin. The table below collects them.

| Model component | Paper symbol | Value (boys / girls) | Source location |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weight equation (`fsig`, `flogis`, `bw`) | Eq. (2) | -- | Methods, "A model for weight", Eq. (2) |
| `lbwmax_male`, `lbwmax_female` | WMAX | 8.42 / 8.22 kg | Table 2 |
| `ltmat50_male`, `ltmat50_female` | PMA50 | 44.13 / 44.88 weeks | Results paragraph 2 (Table 2: 44.1 / 44.8) |
| `lhill_male`, `lhill_female` | $\gamma$ | 4.53 / 4.11 | Table 2; Results paragraph 2 |
| `lkgrow` | $\alpha$ | 0.003299 /week (both sexes) | Table 2 |
| `llogismax_male`, `llogismax_female` | $\alpha/\beta$ | 14.3 / 12.7 | Table 2 |
| `propSd` | $\sigma$ (CV) | 17.9% | Table 2, "Residual variability" |
| No IIV | -- | -- | Results paragraph 1 ("only one measurement per patient") |
| Sex selection via `SEXF` | gender | -- | Results paragraph 2; Table 2 |

## Units

| Symbol | Units | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `time` / `pma` | week | the rxode2 time variable **is** postmenstrual age |
| `bw`, `bwmax` | kg | |
| `tmat50` | week | PMA at half of `bwmax` in the sigmoid component |
| `hill` | unitless | |
| `kgrow` | 1/week | |
| `logismax` | unitless | maximum of the logistic factor, $\alpha/\beta$ |
| `propSd` | fraction | |

# Parameter table

```{r param-table, echo = FALSE}
ui$iniDf |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(.data$ntheta)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Parameter = .data$name,
    Estimate = signif(ifelse(grepl("^l", .data$name), exp(.data$est), .data$est), 4),
    Label = .data$label
  ) |>
  dplyr::rename("Value (back-transformed)" = "Estimate") |>
  knitr::kable()
```

# Simulation

## Typical curves

The typical weight does not depend on the residual error, so `bw` is read
directly from the solve. One "subject" per sex is solved on a weekly PMA grid
spanning the fitted range.

```{r simulate}
mod <- readModelDb("Guk_2017_bodyWeight")

solve_sex <- function(sexf, pma) {
  ev <- data.frame(id = 1L, time = pma, evid = 0L, SEXF = sexf)
  out <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod, ev, returnType = "data.frame")
  out$SEXF <- sexf
  out$sex <- ifelse(sexf == 1, "Girl", "Boy")
  out
}

pma_grid <- seq(25, 718, by = 1)
typ <- dplyr::bind_rows(solve_sex(0, pma_grid), solve_sex(1, pma_grid))
nrow(typ)
```

```{r fig4, fig.cap = "Typical body weight against PMA for boys and girls. Replicates the median prediction lines of Figure 4 of Guk 2017."}
ggplot(typ, aes(.data$time, .data$bw, linetype = .data$sex)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "PMA (weeks)", y = "Weight (kg)", linetype = "Sex") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Stochastic cohort

A cross-sectional virtual cohort has 200 children per sex at each of eight PMAs,
one weight each with the proportional residual error, as in the source data.

```{r stochastic}
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20170601)
pma_vpc <- c(30, 40, 60, 100, 200, 400, 600, 700)
n_per_sex <- 200
cohort <- expand.grid(id = seq_len(2 * n_per_sex), time = pma_vpc) |>
  dplyr::mutate(evid = 0L, SEXF = as.integer(.data$id > n_per_sex)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$id, .data$time)

# The model has no between-subject variability by design (one weight per
# child), so rxode2's warning about a multi-subject solve without omega is
# expected and muffled; any other warning still surfaces.
vpc <- withCallingHandlers(
  rxode2::rxSolve(mod, cohort, keep = "SEXF", returnType = "data.frame"),
  warning = function(w) {
    if (grepl("without 'omega'", conditionMessage(w), fixed = TRUE)) {
      invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    }
  }
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(sex = ifelse(.data$SEXF == 1, "Girl", "Boy"))
nrow(vpc)
```

```{r vpc-plot, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Virtual cohort (200 per sex at each PMA) with the typical curves. Compare with the body weight versus PMA panel of Figure 2 and with Figure 3 of Guk 2017."}
ggplot(vpc, aes(.data$time, .data$sim)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 4, alpha = 0.15, size = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = typ, aes(.data$time, .data$bw), colour = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~sex) +
  labs(x = "PMA (weeks)", y = "Body weight (kg)") +
  theme_bw()
```

# Validation

This is an anthropometric model with no drug, so there is no NCA. The checks
below test the equation, the published curves and the residual error.

## 1. The model returns Eq. (2)

The output must equal Eq. (2) evaluated by hand from the paper's numbers. Both
sides use the same values, so any difference is a transcription or algebra
error and the bound is tight.

```{r exact-check}
eq2 <- function(pma, wmax, pma50, gam, alpha, alpha_over_beta) {
  wmax * pma^gam / (pma50^gam + pma^gam) / (exp(-alpha * pma) + 1 / alpha_over_beta)
}
chk <- typ |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$time %in% c(25, 40, 52, 92, 144, 194, 300, 500, 718)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    bw_hand = ifelse(
      .data$SEXF == 1,
      eq2(.data$time, 8.22, 44.88, 4.11, 0.003299, 12.7),
      eq2(.data$time, 8.42, 44.13, 4.53, 0.003299, 14.3)
    )
  )
stopifnot(
  nrow(chk) == 18,
  all(abs(chk$bw - chk$bw_hand) < 1e-8)
)
chk |>
  dplyr::select("sex", "time", "bw") |>
  dplyr::rename("Sex" = "sex", "PMA (weeks)" = "time", "Typical weight (kg)" = "bw") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

At 40 weeks (a term newborn) the typical weights are about 3.5 kg (boys) and
3.3 kg (girls); at 92 weeks (one year after a term birth) about 10 kg.

## 2. Curves against Figure 4

The maintainers read the end of the median prediction lines in Figure 4 by eye:
about 51.5 kg for boys and 47.5 kg for girls at the right edge of the plot
(about 718 weeks). The Discussion also states that boys are heavier than girls
at every PMA. With the published estimates this holds from 34 weeks PMA onwards;
below about 33.7 weeks the girls' lower Hill coefficient makes their typical
weight slightly higher (0.68 versus 0.60 kg at 25 weeks), a region where the two
lines of Figure 4 overlap.

```{r fig4-check}
fig4 <- data.frame(sex = c("Boy", "Girl"), fig4_kg = c(51.5, 47.5))
end_pts <- typ |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$time == 718) |>
  dplyr::select("sex", "bw") |>
  dplyr::left_join(fig4, by = "sex") |>
  dplyr::mutate(pct_diff = 100 * (.data$bw / .data$fig4_kg - 1))

boys <- typ$bw[typ$SEXF == 0 & typ$time >= 34]
girls <- typ$bw[typ$SEXF == 1 & typ$time >= 34]
crossover <- typ$time[typ$SEXF == 1][typ$bw[typ$SEXF == 1] >= typ$bw[typ$SEXF == 0]]
range(crossover)
stopifnot(
  all(abs(end_pts$pct_diff) < 5),
  all(boys > girls),
  max(crossover) < 34
)
end_pts |>
  dplyr::rename(
    "Sex" = "sex", "Model at 718 weeks (kg)" = "bw",
    "Figure 4 (kg, read by eye)" = "fig4_kg", "Difference (%)" = "pct_diff"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

## 3. Median weight at the median PMA (Table 1)

The typical weight increases monotonically with PMA, so for one sex the median
of the predictions equals the prediction at the median PMA. Table 1 gives a
median PMA of 193.9 weeks and a median weight of 14.0 kg for the pooled cohort.
The sex-weighted typical weight at 193.9 weeks should be close to 14.0 kg. A
mis-transcribed WMAX or $\alpha/\beta$ would move it by more than the 5%
tolerance.

```{r table1-check}
med <- dplyr::bind_rows(solve_sex(0, 193.9), solve_sex(1, 193.9))
bw_pooled <- 0.567 * med$bw[med$SEXF == 0] + 0.433 * med$bw[med$SEXF == 1]
stopifnot(abs(bw_pooled / 14.0 - 1) < 0.05)
data.frame(
  quantity = c("Boys", "Girls", "Pooled (56.7% boys)", "Table 1 median weight"),
  kg = c(med$bw[med$SEXF == 0], med$bw[med$SEXF == 1], bw_pooled, 14.0)
) |>
  dplyr::rename("Typical weight at PMA 193.9 weeks" = "quantity", "kg" = "kg") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

## 4. The sigmoid component saturates by two years of age

The Discussion states that the sigmoid component "only exerts a significant
role in describing the change in weight up to 2 year-old". At 144 weeks PMA (two
years after a term birth) the sigmoid factor should be essentially at its
maximum for both sexes.

```{r sigmoid-check}
sig <- typ |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$time == 144) |>
  dplyr::select("sex", "fsig")
stopifnot(all(sig$fsig > 0.99))
sig |>
  dplyr::rename("Sex" = "sex", "Sigmoid factor at 144 weeks" = "fsig") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

## 5. Residual variability of the stochastic cohort

The spread of `sim / pred` in the virtual cohort must recover the 17.9% CV.
Both sides come from the same draw, so the only difference is Monte-Carlo error;
with 1,600 draws per sex the standard error of the SD is about 2% of its value.

```{r cv-check}
cv_chk <- vpc |>
  dplyr::group_by(.data$sex) |>
  dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n(), cv_sim = stats::sd(.data$sim / .data$bw), .groups = "drop")
stopifnot(
  all(cv_chk$n == n_per_sex * length(pma_vpc)),
  all(abs(cv_chk$cv_sim / 0.179 - 1) < 0.10)
)
cv_chk |>
  dplyr::rename("Sex" = "sex", "N draws" = "n", "Simulated CV" = "cv_sim") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

# Assumptions and deviations

* **PMA is the time axis.** The rxode2 `time` variable is PMA in weeks; the
  model has no dosing and no ODE states. To use it as a covariate generator,
  solve it on the PMA grid of interest (PMA = gestational age at birth +
  postnatal age, both in weeks) and pass `bw` on as `WT`. The fit covers 24.6
  to 718.3 weeks (children under 12 years); the authors caution against
  extrapolating to adolescents.
* **PMA50 uses the two-decimal values of the Results text.** The Results give
  44.13 weeks (boys) and 44.88 weeks (girls); Table 2 prints 44.1 and 44.8,
  which are the same values truncated to one decimal. The difference in
  predicted weight is under 0.3%.
* **Sex-specific values are encoded directly.** Table 2 reports a separate
  estimate for each sex rather than a covariate coefficient, so the model
  carries one parameter per sex and selects it with `SEXF`. The large RSEs of
  the girls' rows (for example 37.2% for WMAX) suggest the girls' values were
  estimated as a shift from the boys' values; that parameterisation is not
  reported and does not change the typical curves.
* **Boys versus girls below 34 weeks PMA.** The Discussion says boys are
  heavier at every PMA, but the published estimates give girls a slightly
  higher typical weight below about 33.7 weeks PMA (very preterm infants). The
  values are kept as published and not adjusted.
* **Residual error.** Table 2 labels the residual row "$\sigma^2$ (CV %)" with
  the value 17.9; it is read as a proportional error with a CV of 17.9%
  (`propSd = 0.179`). The Results state that a combined error model was tried
  and the additive part was negligible.
* **Not extracted:** the candidate sigmoid-times-exponential model (Eq. 1),
  which was rejected on AIC and whose estimates are not reported.
